title: Sub 3-hour marathon runners for five consecutive decades demonstrate a reduced age-related decline in performance
authors: Lepers R, Burfoot A, Stapley PJ
population: 40 sub-3-h marathoners (39 males, 1 female), best marathon per calendar decade from the 1970s to 2010s; mean PB 2:23 +/- 0:09 at age 28.6 +/- 4.7
findings: The time difference between personal best and worst marathon performance in the 5th (calendar) decade was 26 +/- 9 min, an increase of 1 min 4 s per year, i.e. a decrease in running speed of 0.67 +/- 0.29% per year.
With consistent training and racing it may be possible to limit the age-related decline in marathon performance to less than 7% per decade at least until 60 years of age.
World-record-based estimates of decline are limited because records belong to different individuals; longitudinal data on the same individuals are more appropriate.
The authors say further studies are required to verify whether such a low rate could be maintained after 60.
limitations: Tiny, self-selected cohort of elite-level survivors, nearly all male; not representative of recreational runners; abstract defines the decline via best vs worst performance in the last decade, not an age-matched population curve.
implications: For a consistently training runner, an optimistic upper bound on marathon speed retention is about 0.67% per year (under 7% per decade) through about 60; only 0.67% appears in the abstract, the 0.5% lower figure was not supported and is dropped.
Do not apply this rate as a default for athletes with inconsistent training; condition the slope on training consistency (weeks completed per year).

verification.notes: Crossref and Europe PMC abstract match. Researcher's '0.5-0.7%' range corrected to the single reported 0.67 +/- 0.29%; clarified that '5th decade' is the calendar decade (mean age at first PB about 28.6, last decade about 61).
